newsitem.title: CHINA: China-ruled Hong Kong set to freeze labour rights.
newsitem.headline: China-ruled Hong Kong set to freeze labour rights.

text.p: Hong Kong's new government is set to push through a bill rolling back labour rights laws in a move that could spark a new constitutional conflict.

The suspension of labour bills that have been tailored to international standards would be the second move in a week to lay the post-colonial government open to charges it has violated Hong Kong's new constitution, the Basic Law.

The Provisional Legislative Council, sitting on Wednesday, is almost certain to rubber stamp the government bill, freezing seven pre-handover laws until September so the administration can draft counter-laws, political analysts said.
Two weeks ago Britain handed Hong Kong, a colony for 156 years, back to Beijing as a Special Administrative Region of China. China has pledged the territory would undergo virtually no change.
But the philosophy of government is evolving fast, political analysts said, with China-appointed leader Tung Chee-hwa trying to use the appointed legislature as a rubber stamp.
Last Wednesday the council approved a government bill allowing the deportation of thousands of child illegal immigrants to mainland China even if they have ultimate residency rights here.
The move has galvanised the legal profession into action to attack the government for violating children's constitutional rights to residency through having a parent in Hong Kong.
If the government loses that case, the legal system could be plunged into chaos, legal experts have said. And now, a second potential constitutional mess is emerging, they added.

A week before the flag change, pro-democracy legislators and union bosses in the former elected Legislative Council passed the labour rights laws, bringing local labour law into line with international labour conventions.
The laws grant unions the power to bargain collectively with employers on behalf of employees on wages and benefits, and the right to use funds for non-labour activities.

The Basic Law, promulgated by China for post-colonial Hong Kong seven years before the handover, states in its 39th article that standards set by the Geneva-based international labour conventions shall apply in the territory.

"I think there's a constitutional issue that's going to arise if the sponsors of the labour bills or the unions challenge this move," Hong Kong University professor and human rights law expert Nihal Jayawickrama told Reuters.
"The bill on collective bargaining seeks to implement the international labour conventions. Under article 39 of the Basic Law, those rights are now entrenched," Jayawickrama said.
"They can't be taken away, there would be a conflict with the Basic Law," he said.

Protests against the government's move continued on Tuesday as labour groups and pro-democracy legislators staged 48-hour sit-ins outside subway train stations and collected signatures on a petition to oppose the labour rights freeze.
Labour leader Leung Yiu-chung declared he was on hunger strike, taking over from union boss Lee Cheuk-yan who ended a five-day protest fast on Monday.
Labour groups plan to hand over petitions to Tung's office on Wednesday and to stage a rally as the legislature's session begins.
Writing in the South China Morning Post, popular political columnist Andy Ho said the post-handover honeymoon was over.
"Recent moves by Mr Tung have made it increasingly difficult for even more tolerant citizens to give the new administration the benefit of the doubt," Ho wrote.
